messages.subject: Re: levels/groups on axis strings
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way, but it may not be what you want aesthetically. The idea is to create sub-panels for the nested levels.

*Reproducible example*   (!!!)

dd <- data.frame(fac1 = factor(rep(c("I", "II", "III"), each = 60)),
                  fac2 = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), c(40, 20))),
                  fac3 = factor(rep(letters[1:3], each = 20)),
                  fac4 = factor(rep(c("w1", "w2"), each = 10)),
                     y = rnorm(180))

ggplot(dd, aes(x = fac3, y = y, color = fac4)) +
    geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1)) +
    facet_grid(. ~ fac1 + fac2, scales = "free_x")

I'd prefer to visualize the nesting of fac2 within fac1 by having a solid fac1 level strip across all levels of fac2, but AFAIK that isn't implemented in ggplot2 at present.

Dennis

messages.subject: Can somebody help me to implement following plotting style?
messages.subject_clean: Can somebody help me to implement following plotting style?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was trying to achieve following style as in
'http://stackoverflow.com/questions/12675147/how-can-we-make-xkcd-style-graphs-in-r'.
Below are the underlying codes:

library(ggplot2)
library(extrafont)

### Already have read in fonts (see previous answer on how to do this)
loadfonts()

### Set up the trial dataset
data <- NULL
data$x <- seq(1, 10, 0.1)
data$y1 <- sin(data$x)
data$y2 <- cos(data$x)
data$xaxis <- -1.5

data <- as.data.frame(data)

### XKCD theme
theme_xkcd <- theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill="white"),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour=NA),
    panel.grid = element_line(colour="white"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour=NA),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour="black"),
    text = element_text(size=16, family="Humor Sans")
    )

 ### Plot the chart
 p <- ggplot(data=data, aes(x=x, y=y1))+
      geom_line(aes(y=y2), position="jitter")+
      geom_line(colour="white", size=3, position="jitter")+
      geom_line(colour="red", size=1, position="jitter")+
      geom_text(family="Humor Sans", x=6, y=-1.2, label="A SIN AND COS CURVE")+
      geom_line(aes(y=xaxis), position = position_jitter(h = 0.005),
colour="black")+
      scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(2, 5, 6, 9),
      labels = c("YARD", "STEPS", "DOOR", "INSIDE"))+labs(x="", y="")+
      theme_xkcd

However I am not getting the 'Humor Sans' font-effect. I am getting
following Warning message:

> p
Warning messages:
1: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
2: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
3: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
4: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
5: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
6: In grid.Call.graphics(L_text, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database
7: In grid.Call(L_textBounds, as.graphicsAnnot(x$label), x$x, x$y,  :
  Font family not found in Windows font database

However I have checked that, I have installed the font 'Humor Sans'
onto my machine (i.e. this font is there in the 'Windows -->> Fonts'
folder). I am using R 2.15.1 in Windows 7 machine.

Can somebody help me where my implementation went wrong?

Thanks and regards,

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You could open an issue at https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues and make it clear that your wishlist item has to do with nested sets of factor levels. If it's possible to extend the formula notation to embrace nested factors, e.g., facet_wrap( ~ A/B) [B nested within A], that would be even better, but I imagine that some parts of the code might break with such an extension. Just a thought....

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Inequality plots
messages.body_plain:
For this particular problem, you could do the following:

linymax <- 3
ggplot(dta, aes(x = Indep, y = Dep)) +
     geom_line(size = linymax) +
     geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Dep, ymax = Inf), fill = "blue", alpha = 0.3) +
     scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
     scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, linymax))

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Wed, Dec 5, 2012 at 8:35 PM, pharmpk <yanxia...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear users,
>
> I am using ggplot2 version 0.8.9 and I am encountering an error message "Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'Lower' not found" with the following code to draw a graph with ribbons and points,
>
> ggplot(qSum,aes(x=TSLD,ymin=Lower,ymax=Upper))+geom_ribbon(alpha=0.5,fill="blue")+
> geom_point(data=nmData2,aes(TSLD,CONC))+
> facet_wrap(~STDY,scales = "free")

Notice that you defined ymin and ymax as aesthetics in the *base* ggplot; it will expect to find these aesthetics in all subsequent layers. Redo the code as follows:

ggplot(qSum, aes(x = TSLD, y = CONC)) +
   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), fill = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
   geom_point() +
   facet_wrap(~ STDY, scales = "free")

In this form. the common aesthetics are x and y, while ymin and ymax are specific to geom_ribbon().

>
> The weird thing is that if remove the geom_point line, it works and the code is able to draw ribbons:
>
> ggplot(qSum,aes(x=TSLD,ymin=Lower,ymax=Upper))+geom_ribbon(alpha=0.5,fill="blue")+
> #geom_point(data=nmData2,aes(TSLD,CONC))+
> facet_wrap(~STDY,scales = "free")
>
> It was also confirmed that without geom_ribbon, the code for geom_points also works. Can anyone help to figure out what is the problem here. Thanks in advance!
>
> qSum data looks like this

Presenting data of the form below in an e-mail is not productive; it's better to
(a) dput() an R data object and either paste the result from the console to the e-mail or export it to a text file and attach it to the e-mail; e.g., dput(qSum)
(b) create plain text files such as csv files and attach them to the e-mail, or
(c) if large, save the data object as an R binary with a .Rdata extension and attach to the mail; e.g. save(qSum, file = "qSum.Rdata")

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Violinplot and discrete values
messages.body_plain:
You can use the "adjust" parameter, like geom_violin(adjust=2).

Since geom_violin uses (by default) stat_ydensity, you can look in ?stat_ydensity - this in turn will point you to ?density, since that's the function that does the actual calculation.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
You need to use xintercept, and convert it to numeric:

ggplot(tasks, aes(xmin = Start, xmax = End, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymin+ 1, fill = Process)) +
geom_rect() +
facet_grid(Workstream.ID+Workstream.Name+SubSubProject+SubProject+SMC.PI~.) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept=as.numeric(today)))+

theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
labs(x="Year")

The conversion to numeric is probably a bug. Could you file it on github?
Thanks!
-Winston

> loess. Use 'method = x' to change the smoothing method.\

The default smoothing method in geom_smooth() is loess.

The formula is unnecessary - method = lm is sufficient. Had the
formula been necessary, you would need to have used formula = y ~ x.
ggplot2 will map y to X1 and x to X2 internally.

Dennis

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.9.3 released!
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

We're pleased to announce the release of ggplot2 0.9.3! ggplot2 uses the scales and gtable packages, and there are also new versions of these packages: scales 0.2.3 and gtable 0.1.2. The source and binary versions should be available on the CRAN mirrors by now. To get the latest version of ggplot2 and all its dependencies, start a clean R session and run `install.packages("ggplot2", dep = T)`.

Most of the changes in this version are bug fixes. Perhaps the most visible change is that ggplot will now print out warning messages when you use `stat="bin"` and also map a variable to y. For example, these are valid:

    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
    ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl)) + geom_bar(stat = "bin")

But these will result in some warnings:

    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_bar(stat = "bin")
    # The default stat for geom_bar is "bin", so this is the same as above:
    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_bar()

The reason for this change is to make behavior more consistent -- `stat_bin` generates a y value, and so should not work when you also map a value to y.

For a full list of changes, please see: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggplot2/NEWS

Regards,

Winston & Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Control Significant Figures in Mean Lables
messages.subject_clean: Control Significant Figures in Mean Lables
messages.body_plain:
On 12/6/2012 8:20 AM, jrr wrote:
> How do I control the number of significant figures in labels created by the
> following?
>                       stat_summary(aes(label=..fun..), fun.y=mean,
> geom="text", size=2)
> Thanks

Either

stat_summary(aes(label=signif(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean, geom="text", size=2)

or

stat_summary(aes(label=round(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean, geom="text", size=2)

depending on whether you really mean significant figures or digits after
the decimal point. See the appropriate help page for signif and round if
you are not sure.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: Plot points into DEM: "Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale"
messages.subject_clean: Plot points into DEM: "Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale"
messages.body_plain:
Diego,

I didn't run your code, but am pretty sure the problem is that you're
already defined a continuous fill (Altitud) in the geom_tile call, and
then are trying to have a separate discrete fill (Estacion) in
geom_point. This can't be done as far as I know, see e.g.:
https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/ggplot2/lDvsd4yJ0AE

What about just setting color to Estacion in geom_point? (And
obviously removing the color="black" setting.) Would this give the
effect you want? Otherwise, perhaps re-think this plot and what you're
trying to show.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Follow-up:

After reading Winston's post in another thread, I started a new
session and reinstalled ggplot2 and plyr (along with evaluate, gtable
and scales just to be sure :). I then tried
Maga's example again:

> library(ggplot2)
> library(plyr)

> df <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(letters[1:3], each = 10)),
+                  y = rnorm(30))
> # Compute sample mean and standard deviation in each group
> library(plyr)
> ds <- ddply(df, .(gp), summarise, mean = mean(y), sd = sd(y))
>
> # Declare the data frame and common aesthetics.
> # The summary data frame ds is used to plot
> # larger red points in a second geom_point() layer.
> # If the data = argument is not specified, it uses the
> # declared data frame from ggplot(); ditto for the aesthetics.
> ggplot(df, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
+     geom_point() +
+     geom_point(data = ds, aes(y = mean),
+                colour = 'red', size = 3)
>

The plot now renders fine and there are no messages in the console, as
the above copy/paste from the console shows. (Note the screen prompt
at the end of the snippet.) Thanks to Winston for the explanation at
the RStudio blog - I imagine it's been a hectic day or two for him
replying to all of these inquiries...

Dennis

messages.subject: Price-volume plot with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Let say I have the followings data:

Dat1 = structure(list(Date = structure(c(15670, 15671, 15672, 15673,
+ 15674, 15677, 15678, 15679, 15680, 15670, 15671, 15672, 15673,
+ 15674, 15677, 15678, 15679, 15680), class = "Date"), Price = c(37.47,
+ 37.34, 37.97, 38.34, 38.29, 37.92, 38.13, 38.66, 38.32, 33.97,
+ 33.62, 33.62, 33.93, 34.13, 34.14, 33.92, 33.91, 33.65), Volume = c(3283000,
+ 3435400, 3454000, 3970800, 2406200, 2714500, 2188400, 3927500,
+ 3568700, 34852800, 26506100, 30828500, 29542600, 36130600, 19611800,
+ 21290900, 29170900, 23415000), Asset = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L,
+ 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("A",
+ "B"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("Date", "Price", "Volume",
+ "Asset"), row.names = c(NA, 18L), class = "data.frame")

Now with this data, I would like to have a plot as given in
'http://www.simple-talk.com/content/print.aspx?article=1351' (please
see the first plot).

Basically in my plot there will be 2 parts in my plotting window. In
the upper part, I will have price-series (just time series plot). And
in the lower part, I will plot the Volumes (as small bar-charts). And
2 Assets "A" & "B" will be distinguished by 2 different colors.

Can somebody throw me some pointer how to achieve that with ggplot?

Thanks for your help.

messages.subject: Re: Price-volume plot with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You don't have enough information to do the top plot - you need the
daily min and max as well as the opening value to associate with the
tick. Those values are not represented in Dat1 - I don't know what
Price represents. Basically, you would need to apply geom_segment()
for both the vertical range and the horizontal tick in the price
chart. The bar chart would be much simpler in principle. A few things:

(i) The y-axis for both plots will be on the left rather than the right.
(ii) You'll need to make some adjustments to compensate for the large
difference in value ranges between price and volume, because by
default the two y-axis lines will not be aligned.
(iii) Use scale_x_date() to attune the date scale (you may need to use
the scales package).
(iv) Look into grid.arrange() in gridExtra or the approach used in
section 8.4 of the ggplot2 book to stitch the two plots together.

This should already be available in the quantmod or xts packages, but
if you're just curious about how it can be done in ggplot2, it's
certainly possible and not all that hard.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Price-volume plot with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Christopher,

I see Dennis's response noting there's not enough data here, but when
you have all the required data, you'll want to first generate the two
plots, and then, as he notes, use something like gridExtra to arrange
them on a page. Just using the data you posted, e.g.:

# Hi-lo plot
p1 <- ggplot(Dat1,aes(Date,Price)) +
stat_summary(fun.ymax="max",fun.ymin="min",geom="pointrange",fun.y="mean")

# Volume plot
p2 <- ggplot(Dat1,aes(Date,Volume,group=Asset))+geom_bar(aes(fill=Asset),stat="identity")

# Dark ages example: arrange using grid, not gridExtra
library( grid )
grid.newpage()
pushViewport( viewport( layout=grid.layout( 3, 1 ) ) )
vplayout<-function( x, y ) viewport( layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y )
print( p1, vp=vplayout( 1:2,1 ) )
print( p2, vp=vplayout( 2, 1 ) )

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Price-volume plot with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Dec 7, 2012 at 12:14 PM, Christofer Bogaso
<bogaso.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks Dennis for your suggestion.
>
> However just to mention that, I do not need max-min plotting. That is
> why I said, I just need the the ****Time series plot for the
> Price"""". Means, in the top part just the Time series and in the
> bottom part just the bar plot.

OK. Here are a couple of ways you could go, which will illustrate some
of the issues that arise with trading days as dates, as well as
legends and scales. I'm using the technique outlined in section 8.4 of
the ggplot2 book to size the two plots. There's a way to do this in
gridExtra::grid.arrange() as well, but I don't have the time to
investigate it right now.

## Stab 1: Treat dates as 'numeric'

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)   # needed for the plot layouts below

In this version of the plot, the legend for lines was pulled inside
the graph and the legend for the bar chart was suppressed. By default,
there will be a separate legend for each plot because Asset is mapped
to different aesthetics. I am also plotting volume in millions in an
attempt to align the dates on the plots. Otherwise, the borders of the
two graphs would not be aligned without resorting to trickery.

p1 <- ggplot(Dat1, aes(x = Date, y = Price, colour = Asset)) +
           theme_bw() +
           geom_line(aes(group = Asset), size = 1) + labs(x = "") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                 legend.position = c(0.85, 0.5))

p2 <- ggplot(Dat1, aes(x = Date, y = Volume/1e6, fill = Asset)) +
           theme_bw() +
           geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
           labs(y = "Volume (millions)") +
           scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m/%d")) +
           scale_fill_discrete(guide = "none")

# Set up a grid graphics page
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

# Define a function to set up the layout of the two plots
vplayout <- function(x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

# Print them
print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:15, 1))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(15:20, 1))

The obvious problem with this plot is the missing days on the weekends
and there is no easy way around this if one wants to maintain
'continuous' time. Since the non-trading days are not represented in
Dat1, ggplot2's default in line graphs is to connect the missing dates
with a linear interpolator, which will be constant if Friday's closing
price is equal to Monday's opening price. OTOH, the missing dates in
the bar chart will create gaps.

 Another problem is that the dates are not perfectly aligned: the
points in the line graph align with the left edge of the bars, while
the vertical grid lines in the bar chart line up with the centers of
the bars.

# Stab 2:  convert Date to a factor

This time, create a new factor in Dat1 corresponding to dates and redo
the plots. This time the default legends are kept in the result for
reference.

Dat1$Date2 <- factor(format(Dat1$Date, "%m/%d"))

p3 <- ggplot(Dat1, aes(x = Date2, y = Price, colour = Asset)) +
           theme_bw() +
           geom_line(aes(group = Asset), size = 1) + labs(x = "") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
p4 <- ggplot(Dat1, aes(x = Date2, y = Volume/1e6, fill = Asset)) +
           theme_bw() +
           geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
           labs(y = "Volume (millions)")

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(20, 1)))

print(p3, vp = vplayout(1:15, 1))
print(p4, vp = vplayout(15:20, 1))

You could play with scale_x_discrete() in p4 if you wanted to reduce
the number of factor levels plotted (see the breaks = argument), but
for long series, this might be problematic - e.g., if you wanted to
label the first trading day of a week or month, you would probably
need an indicator in the data set for that property and use it in
defining the breaks = argument of the scale_ function.

There are tools in place to produce something more visually appealing
like the graphics in quantmod, PerformanceAnalytics or xts, but it
would take a bit of work to get there (e.g., a new theme function for
this class of graphic, and perhaps a customized date scale and/or
legend guide).

Hope this is enough to get you started...
Dennis

I made a few adjustments to your code, but the primary change was to explicitly define the shapes using scale_shape_manual().

library(ggplot2)
world<-map_data('world')

myData <- data.frame(coordsx=c(98.6121321,  76.7864778,  92.7209357,
                               0.7608332,   1.6000000,  45.3177332, 102.0901371,
                               76.5475929, -3.9295275, -2.8162432),
                     coordsy=c(50.759610, 25.029751, 53.080824, 25.063100,
                               22.258565, 57.669511, 56.457415, 57.525077,
                               57.546489, -7.682919),
                     myShapes = rep(c('A', 'B'), each = 5) )

(myMap<- ggplot(legend=FALSE) +
   geom_polygon(data=world, aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group), fill='darkgrey') +
   geom_point(data=myData, aes(coordsx, coordsy, shape=myShapes), size=4) +
   theme(panel.background=element_blank(),
         panel.grid.major=element_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor=element_blank()) +
   coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-30,170),
                   ylim=c(-70,90)) +
   labs(x='Latitude', y='Longitude') +
   scale_shape_manual(values = c(2, 1), guide = "none")
)

In the geom_point() layer, notice that shape is inside aes() as it should be, since myShapes is a variable to be mapped to shape. In contrast, size = 4 is *set* to a constant value, which is outside the aes() statement. Now that shape is mapped, by default a legend will be drawn; scale_shape_manual() gives you control over which shapes correspond to which groups (the values = statement) and guide = "none" suppresses the legend for shape.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Control Significant Figures in Mean Lables
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Brian. I am having some difficulty with the documentation of ggplot2. If I ?signif I get help for base R function. However, if I ?label I get nothing. Where are the "aes(label=" parameters documented, and the special variable ..fun.. and other special variables.?  The R help documentation of aes is very cursory, as is the documentation for stat_summary, and other ggplot2 aspects. It seems that one must get most documentation from user groups.

On Thursday, December 6, 2012 4:20:59 PM UTC-5, Brian Diggs wrote:
> On 12/6/2012 8:20 AM, jrr wrote:
> > How do I control the number of significant figures in labels created by the
> > following?
> >                       stat_summary(aes(label=..fun..), fun.y=mean,
> > geom="text", size=2)
> > Thanks
>
> Either
>
> stat_summary(aes(label=signif(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean, geom="text", size=2)
>
> or
>
> stat_summary(aes(label=round(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean, geom="text", size=2)
>
> depending on whether you really mean significant figures or digits after
> the decimal point. See the appropriate help page for signif and round if
> you are not sure.
>
> --
> Brian S. Diggs, PhD
> Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
> Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject_clean: sorting and ordering bars in a ggplot2 bar chart.
messages.body_plain:
I agree with the stackoverflow responders that the question isn't
completely clear. Nonetheless something like this may help...it
produces an order bar graph by your domain and category variables:

# 1. Summarize the data
library(plyr)
d2 <- ddply(ex1.dta,.(category,domain),summarise,grouping=sum(grouping))

# 2. Reorder and create a new x axis label
d3 <- d2[order(d2$category,d2$grouping),]  # reorder
d3$catdom <- paste(d3$category,d3$domain)  # make a new plotting var
d3$catdom <- factor(d3$catdom,levels=d3$catdom)

# 3. Plot
qplot(catdom,grouping,fill=category,data=d3,geom="bar",stat="identity")+theme(axis.text.x
= element_text(angle = 90))

Ben

messages.subject: Installation issues with ggplot2 0.9.3
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

A number of people have mentioned seeing messages like this after updating to ggplot2 0.9.3:
  "The following `from` values were not present in `x`: col, color, pch, cex, lty, lwd, srt, adj, bg, fg, min, max ..."

The cause of these has something to do with the packages not getting properly updated by install.packages(). We haven't pinpointed exactly the circumstances where this happens, but most, if not all, cases happen under Windows. If you are experiencing these problems try the following:

- Start a clean R session, without ggplot2 or plyr loaded. When you run sessionInfo(), you shouldn't see either of these packages listed.
- Run install.packages(c("ggplot2", "gtable", "scales", "plyr"))
- Once they are installed, test it with: library(ggplot2); qplot(1:3, 1:3)

You hopefully will not see any of the error messages at this point.

For further information and discussion with others who have had these problems, please see:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13765835/unusual-error-in-all-ggplot2-commands
http://blog.rstudio.org/2012/12/06/ggplot2-plyr-release/ (in the comments)
https://github.com/hadley/plyr/issues/122

Good luck!
-Winston

recently updated packages in a fresh R session. The statement is a
message, not an error, so working graphs should still render, but that
message gets annoying in a hurry. Suggestion:

(i) start a new R session with no packages other than the standard autoloads;
(ii) install.packages(c("ggplot2", "plyr", "gtable", "scales"))
(iii) try a simple plot like qplot(1:3, 1:3) - the message should now be gone.

As far as Mike's message goes, I downloaded the ggthemes package from
Github late last week and have had no problems using it. Did you read
the download directions in the README.md file? The simplest way, which
does not require compilation, is to have the latest version of
devtools installed and do

library("devtools")
install_github("ggthemes", "jrnold")

This is what worked for me. The other option is to download the tar
ball to your machine and follow the instructions in README.md; it
doesn't appear you did as instructed.

messages.subject: Re: disconnected contours with geom_contour()+coord_polar()
messages.body_plain:
I was able to hack a solution by computing the tiles by hand then using coord() instead of coord_polar(). The following function is very application specific (assumes names of data columns, range of plot, etc), but may be useful to others that encounter this issue in the future:

    polar_plot = function(data){
        dtheta = diff(sort(unique(data$theta)))[1]/2
        dphi = diff(sort(unique(data$phi)))[1]/2
        data$theta_lo = data$theta - dtheta
        data$theta_hi = data$theta + dtheta
        data$phi_lo = data$phi - dphi
        data$phi_hi = data$phi + dphi
        data$theta_lo[data$theta==min(data$theta)] = min(data$theta)
        data$theta_hi[data$theta==max(data$theta)] = max(data$theta)
        data$phi_lo[data$phi==min(data$phi)] = min(data$phi)
        data$phi_hi[data$phi==max(data$phi)] = max(data$phi)
        p = ggplot()+
        geom_rect(
            data = data

            , mapping = aes(
                x = theta
                , y = phi

                , xmin = theta_lo
                , xmax = theta_hi
                , ymin = phi_lo
                , ymax = phi_hi
                , fill = value
                , colour = value
            )
        )+
        coord(
            xlim=c(-180,180)
            , ylim = c(0,90)
            , subclass = 'polar'
            , theta = 'x'
            , r = 'y'
            , start = 0
            , direction = 1
        )
        return(p)
    }
    data = expand.grid(
        phi = c(0,1)
        , theta = c(-180,-90,0,90,180)
    )
    data$value = rnorm(nrow(data))
    polar_plot(data)

ggplot2 is not doing anything unusual. You mapped a numeric vector on
the x axis, and did not change the default x-axis scale, so you got a
plot where the x-axis intervals map to the numeric difference between
each successive x-axis value. If that's not what you want you can
change it--either by telling ggplot to ignore the numeric values of
Workload (as Adam suggested) or by using a log scale (as baptiste
suggested)--but it is the reasonable default.

messages.subject: Re: Control Significant Figures in Mean Lables
messages.subject_clean: Control Significant Figures in Mean Lables
messages.body_plain:
On 12/10/2012 5:01 AM, jrr wrote:
> Thank you Brian. I am having some difficulty with the documentation
> of ggplot2. If I ?signif I get help for base R function.

That's the one that I was referring to.

> However, if I ?label I get nothing. Where are the "aes(label="
> parameters documented, and the special variable ..fun.. and other
> special variables.? The R help documentation of aes is very cursory,
> as is the documentation for stat_summary, and other ggplot2 aspects.
> It seems that one must get most documentation from user groups.

Since label is the name of an argument, it is not surprising that it
does not have its own help page. The help for aes is sparse; the
descriptions of the various aesthetics and what they are/do are in
aes_colour_fill_alpha, aes_group_order, aes_linetype_size_shape, and
aes_position. Unfortunately, label is not described in any of these. The
geoms also have documentation (well, examples) about their individual
aesthetics. For geom_text, label is the actual characters/text drawn or
written.

I could not find any documentation about the special variables in the
standard online documentation. The relevant statement from the ggplot2
book, page 58-59, is:

   The names of generated variables [by stats] must be surrounded with
   .. when used. This prevents confusion in case the original dataset
   includes a variable with the same name as a generated variable, and
   it makes it clear to any reader of the code that this variable was
   generated by a stat. Each statistic lists the variables that it
   creates in its documentation.

In stat_summary, the additional columns are documented as fun.data,
fun.ymin, fun.y, and fun.ymax, though in this case, that documentation
is not right. The actual names are either set by the function called
(for fun.data) or are ymin, y, ymax for the other three. (Also, fun.data
takes a vector, not a data.frame, despite the documentation.)

For an example, this is a generic usage of stat_summary:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=cyl, y=mpg)) +
   stat_summary(fun.ymax = max, fun.y = mean, fun.ymin = min)

But with a different geom, different aesthetics can be set:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=cyl, y=mpg)) +
   stat_summary(fun.ymax = max, fun.y = mean, fun.ymin = min,
                geom="text", aes(label=..y.., colour=..ymax..))

Not that this is a necessarily practical graph, but it shows how things
are used.

I agree that this would be hard to put together from the online
documentation.

>
> On Thursday, December 6, 2012 4:20:59 PM UTC-5, Brian Diggs wrote:
>>
>> On 12/6/2012 8:20 AM, jrr wrote:
>>> How do I control the number of significant figures in labels
>>> created by
>> the
>>> following? stat_summary(aes(label=..fun..), fun.y=mean,
>>> geom="text", size=2) Thanks
>>
>> Either
>>
>> stat_summary(aes(label=signif(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean,
>> geom="text", size=2)
>>
>> or
>>
>> stat_summary(aes(label=round(..fun..,4)), fun.y=mean, geom="text",
>> size=2)
>>
>> depending on whether you really mean significant figures or digits
>> after the decimal point. See the appropriate help page for signif
>> and round if you are not sure.
>>
>> -- Brian S. Diggs, PhD Senior Research Associate, Department of
>> Surgery Oregon Health & Science University
>>
>

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

Hi:

On Wed, Dec 12, 2012 at 12:00 AM, eastafri <geor...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks Ben. what I wanted are the stacked bars like the ones from the
> question. Sorry if the initial question was not as clear. But to clarify, I
> wanted a stacked bar chart with the bars along the X-axis ordered  via some
> other variable and in an descending manner. I thought it should be
> straighforward to do this with ggplot2, but it seems to be difficult.

See the reorder() function to arrange the levels of a factor according
to some function of the values of another variable. Here's a simple
reproducible example to illustrate the point:

DF <- data.frame(expand.grid(a = c("I", "II", "III"), b = LETTERS[1:3]),
                   n = rpois(9, 60))
require(ggplot2)

# ascending order of cumulative bar height:
ggplot(DF, aes(x = reorder(a, n, sum), y = n, fill = b)) +
     geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack")

# descending order:
ggplot(DF, aes(x = reorder(a, -n, sum), y = n, fill = b)) +
     geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack")

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Circular range with geom_rect
messages.body_plain:
The issue is that coord_polar isn't really polar; it's more like a
warping of the rectangular space into a circular one. Because of this,
the values don't "wrap around" from negative to positive values.

If you want to plot things that cross over theta=0, then you'll have
to fake it by using two separate pieces, as you described in your
workaround. (Or you could change the origin angle and use labels with
fake values for the theta breaks.)

-Winston

Hi Martin -

There is a theme option, legend.box.just, which controls the
justification of each legend within the overall legend box. However,
there's a bug in the current version where it isn't possible to
control that value. I've fixed it in the development version of
ggplot2, which you can install using devtools:

# First restart R
install.packages("devtools")  # If not already installed
library(devtools)
install_github("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)
packageVersion('ggplot2')  # Should be 0.9.3.99

I've taken your example and simplified it a bit for clarity. In
addition to legend.box.just, look at legend.justification. That
specifies the "anchor point" that is controlled with legend.position.
See here for more information about that:
http://wiki.stdout.org/rcookbook/Graphs/Legends%20(ggplot2)/#changing-the-position-of-the-legend

messages.body_plain:
As for your earlier question about using geom_dotplot... If I
understand you correctly, at each x position, you want to stack across
the different groups. I don't think that it's possible to do that,
though. This is because the stacking with geom_dotplot is done with a
bit of a hack, due to some technical limitations of ggplot2.

I think this code _would_ do what you wanted, if it weren't for the
weird way that stacking is done:

set.seed(909)
dat2 <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=rnorm(90), g=LETTERS[1:2])

# Using dot-density binning
ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=g)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binaxis="y", stackdir="center", binpositions="all",
               stackgroups=TRUE)

# Using histodot binning
ggplot(dat2, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=g)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-4,4,.4)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binaxis="y", stackdir="center", method="histodot",
               stackgroups=TRUE)

The "stacking" is calculated across all the x positions, which isn't
right for this case. It might be possible to fix it, but it would be
non-trivial.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
You could do something like this:

library(ggplot2)
d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), y=factor(sample(0:1, 100, replace=TRUE)))

ggplot(d, aes(x, colour=y)) + geom_density() +

  geom_rug(aes(y=y), position="jitter", sides="b")

The y position isn't actually used, but it will make position_jitter happy.

Hmmm... second try on posting response

I have stumbled around for awhile and have come up with this to improve the syntax on my particular need, which is stair-step inequalities:

library(ggplot2)
library(proto)
# Modified version of ggplot:::stairstep function
stairstepn <- function( data, direction="hv", yvars="y" ) {
  direction <- match.arg( direction, c( "hv", "vh" ) )
  data <- as.data.frame( data )[ order( data$x ), ]
  n <- nrow( data )

  if ( direction == "vh" ) {
    xs <- rep( 1:n, each = 2 )[ -2 * n ]
    ys <- c( 1, rep( 2:n, each = 2 ) )
  } else {
    ys <- rep( 1:n, each = 2 )[ -2 * n ]
    xs <- c( 1, rep( 2:n, each = 2))
  }

  data.frame(
      x = data$x[ xs ]
    , data[ ys, yvars, drop=FALSE ]
    , data[ xs, setdiff( names( data ), c( "x", yvars ) ), drop=FALSE ]
  )
}

stat_stepribbon <- function( mapping=NULL, data=NULL, geom="ribbon", position="identity" ) {
  StatStepribbon$new( mapping=mapping, data=data, geom=geom, position=position )
}

StatStepribbon <- proto(ggplot2:::Stat, {
  objname <- "stepribbon"
  desc <- "Stepwise area plot"
  desc_outputs <- list(
    x = "stepped independent variable",
    ymin = "stepped minimum dependent variable",
    ymax = "stepped maximum dependent variable"
  )
  required_aes <- c( "x", "ymin", "ymax" )

  default_geom <- function(.) GeomRibbon
  default_aes <- function(.) aes( x=..x.., ymin = ..y.., ymax=Inf )

  calculate <- function( ., data, scales, direction = "hv", yvars = c( "ymin", "ymax" ), ...) {
    stairstepn( data = data, direction = direction, yvars = yvars )
  }

  examples <- function(.) {
    DF <- data.frame( x = 1:3, ymin = runif( 3 ), ymax=rep( Inf, 3 ) )
    ggplot( DF, aes( x=x, ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax ) ) + stat_stepribbon()
  }

})

Dear all, Let say I have following plot

Dat <- structure(list(Date = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L,
3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L), .Label = c("12-03-2012", "12-04-2012",
"12-05-2012", "12-06-2012", "12-07-2012"), class = "factor"),
    OBJ = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
    3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("OBJ 1", "OBJ 2", "OBJ 3"
    ), class = "factor"), Time = c(11, 11.25, 11.35, 12.01, 11.14,
    13, 13.25, 13.35, 14.01, 13.14, 14.5, 14.75, 14.85, 15.51,
    14.64)), .Names = c("Date", "OBJ", "Time"), class = "data.frame",
row.names = c(NA,
-15L));

 p <- ggplot(Dat) +
			geom_line(aes(y = Time, x = as.Date(Dat$Date, "%m-%d-%Y"), color =
OBJ), size = 3) +
			scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m-%d-%Y")) +
			ylab(NULL) + xlab(NULL) +
			scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 17))
p

However I would like to have following:

1. In the Y-axis, instead of showing 10, 12, 14 etc, I would like to
have 10.00, 12.00, 14.00 etc (i.e. 2 significant digits)

2. I would like to readjust the Legend's position. Instead of outside
the plot-canvas, I want to have inside it. For this I tried following:

p + guides(guide_legend(label.vjust = .5))

However nothing has happened.

I also want to have some Background color and Border for legend-area

3. I also add one rectangle along the left-most place. Therefore I
tried following:

p + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = as.Date(Dat$Date,
"%m-%d-%Y")[1], ymax = Inf, ymin = -Inf)

However with this I am having following error:
Error: Invalid input: date_trans works with objects of class Date only

Can somebody help me how to achieve these goals.

Thanks for your help.

Hi Chris,

Please see inline below.

On Sun, Dec 16, 2012 at 4:21 AM, Christofer Bogaso

> 3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L), .Label = c("12-03-2012", "12-04-2012",

>     OBJ = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
>     3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("OBJ 1", "OBJ 2", "OBJ 3"
>     ), class = "factor"), Time = c(11, 11.25, 11.35, 12.01, 11.14,
>     13, 13.25, 13.35, 14.01, 13.14, 14.5, 14.75, 14.85, 15.51,
>     14.64)), .Names = c("Date", "OBJ", "Time"), class = "data.frame",
> row.names = c(NA,
> -15L));
>
>  p <- ggplot(Dat) +
>                         geom_line(aes(y = Time, x = as.Date(Dat$Date, "%m-%d-%Y"), color =
> OBJ), size = 3) +
>                         scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m-%d-%Y")) +
>                         ylab(NULL) + xlab(NULL) +
>                         scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 17))
> p

I've rearranged this a little to make things easier later on:

Dat$Date <- as.Date(Dat$Date, "%m-%d-%Y")

 p <- ggplot(Dat, aes(y = Time,
                      x = Date,
                      color = OBJ)) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +

  scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m-%d-%Y")) +
  ylab(NULL) + xlab(NULL)

>

> However I would like to have following:
>
> 1. In the Y-axis, instead of showing 10, 12, 14 etc, I would like to
> have 10.00, 12.00, 14.00 etc (i.e. 2 significant digits)

You can format labels with arbitrary function, e.g.

(p <- p + scale_y_continuous(labels=function(x) sprintf("%1.2f", x)))

>
> 2. I would like to readjust the Legend's position. Instead of outside
> the plot-canvas, I want to have inside it. For this I tried following:
>
> p + guides(guide_legend(label.vjust = .5))
>
> However nothing has happened.

Legend position is set by the theme:

(p <- p + theme(legend.position=c(.2, .8)))

As an aside, for this kind of plot I recommend directlabels:

library(directlabels) #may need to install first
direct.label(p)

>
> I also want to have some Background color and Border for legend-area

Also handled by theme (see ?theme for details)

(p <- p + theme(legend.background = element_rect(fill="green", color="blue")))

>
> 3. I also add one rectangle along the left-most place. Therefore I
> tried following:
>
> p + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = as.Date(Dat$Date,
> "%m-%d-%Y")[1], ymax = Inf, ymin = -Inf)
>

There are a couple of problems here. First (and the likely source of
your error) is that Inf and -Inf are not dates. Even once we get past
that, there we're going to have a problem because values outside of
limits set by scales are discarded. I think you'll have to set the
limits on the coordinates instead. Here is my initial attempt:

(p <- p + annotate("rect",
                   xmin = min(Dat$Date - 10),
                   xmax = min(Dat$Date),
                   ymax = max(Dat$Time + 10),
                   ymin = min(Dat$Time - 10)) +
 coord_cartesian(xlim=c(min(Dat$Date) - 2, max(Dat$Date) + .1),
                 ylim=c(min(Dat$Time) -.5, max(Dat$Time) + .5))
 )

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: stat_density2d with weights
messages.body_plain:
Hi all ggplot2 experts,

I'm doing some stat_density2d() plots with weighted data. What I found out is, that the graphic doesn't change if I am adding a 'weight' variable (as shown in the example)- there is no warning or error, but no change. A toy example/simplification of my 'real problem':

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(17122012)
a <- c(runif(6,0,1), runif(3,2,4))
b <- c(runif(6,0,1), runif(3,2,5))
weights <- rep(c(1.354,20),c(6.045474,3))

df1 <- data.frame(a,b,WEI=weights)

p1 <- ggplot(df1,aes(a,b))
p1 + stat_density2d()

p2 <- ggplot(df1,aes(a,b,weight=WEI))
p2 + stat_density2d()
# they are both the same!

I found out that stat_density2d uses the "kde2d" function which does not permit weights. So, can anybody think of a solution for my problem?
Thank you all!

Manuel

I am trying to plot relative frequencies and I cannot find the way to make such a plot. Please see the code I am using:

    scale_colour_discrete(name = "Classes") +      #
   theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +  # remove graph grids

    labs(x= 'Year', y='Count')                                       # change axis names

The graph is *almost* what I pursue. However, instead of "count" on the y axis, I would like to show relative frequencies. By "relative frequencies" I mean the proportion of each class relative to the total of that year. For example, class 1 (2899) represents 0.73 of 3967 total values in 1996.

Thiago.

messages.subject: Re: Difficulties when trying to plot relative frequencies
messages.subject_clean: Difficulties when trying to plot relative frequencies
messages.body_plain:
I would just calculate the values using plyr and then plot them:

library(plyr)
df <- ddply(df,
            "year",
            transform,
            prop = value/sum(value))

ggplot(df, aes(x=year, y=prop, group=class)) +

  geom_line(aes(colour = as.factor(class))) +
  scale_colour_discrete(name = "Classes") +      #
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +  # remove graph grids
  labs(x= 'Year', y='Count')

HTH,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
If you set your alpha to 0.50 and you're seeing two colors (one darker than the other) then it's because you have points that are being plotted on top of each other. The way around this is to make the graph huge so jitter has plenty of room to separate the points or make your points very small. I wonder if perhaps you'd be better off with a summary of your data rather than plotting every point. Perhaps a boxplot?

messages.body_plain:
Ah, OK, so you have an overplotting problem. If alpha<1 there aren't
two different colors, but obviously when dots overlap the alphas are
additive (indeed, this is the whole point). Other ways to deal with
this include axis transforms, geom_histogram, geom_density2d, and as
Brandon suggested, summarizing your data before plotting.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Doug,

I think you have to change the data, but that should be easy enough.
If you want to replace all the paces with newlines:

Dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(10),
                  y=rnorm(10),
                  Group=rep(c("This string is quite long",
                  "This string is even longer than the other long string"),
                  each=5))

Dat$Group <- gsub(" ", "\n", Dat$Group)

If you want more complicated wrapping you can use str_wrap in the
stringr package:

library(stringr)
Dat$Group <- str_wrap(Dat$Group, width = 20)

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
I'm not opposed to the feature request, but personally I don't really
miss this. If you don't want to modify the original data you can
always do it on the fly:

Dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(10),
                  y=rnorm(10),
                  Group=rep(c("This string is quite long",
                  "This string is even longer than the other long string"),
                  each=5))

library(stringr)

ggplot(transform(Dat,
                 Group = str_wrap(Group,
                                  width = 20)),
       aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~Group)

levels(Dat$Group) ## unchanged in Dat

Of course this is not a good approach is Dat is large, but in many
cases it will work just fine.

HTH,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: Forest plot y-axis in log scale
messages.subject_clean: Forest plot y-axis in log scale
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This seems to work:

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, ymin=ylo, ymax=yhi)) +
    geom_pointrange(size=0.75, shape=18) +

    geom_hline(yintercept=1, linetype="dashed", lwd=0.7) +

    scale_y_log10(name="Odds Ratio", limits = c(0.7, 1.8),

                       breaks=c(0.80, 1.0, 1.20, 1.40, 1.60, 1.80)) +

    coord_flip() +
xlab("Study") +
theme(axis.title = element_text(size=14),
      axis.text = element_text(face="bold", colour="black"))

If you look carefully, you'll see that the log-transformation is
applied because the widths between axis ticks on the (log) odds ratio
scale are not equal. ggplot2 uses the values in the original scale as
the axis ticks but the scale in which they are rendered is log_10,
which you can tell by the spacing between the grid lines. See the
examples at the bottom of
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/scale_continuous.html for further
illustration of this idea.

If you want the plot to be linear in the log10 scale, you could do
something like this:

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=log10(y), ymin=log10(ylo), ymax=log10(yhi))) +
    geom_pointrange(size=0.75, shape=18) +
    geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed", lwd=0.7) +
    scale_y_continuous(name="Log Odds Ratio", limits = c(-0.15, 0.25),
                       breaks= seq(-0.1, 0.2, by = 0.1)) +
    coord_flip() +
    xlab("Study") +
    theme(axis.title = element_text(size=14),
              axis.text = element_text(face="bold", colour="black"))

(Aside: Notice the abridgement of the theme() call - the new theming
system applies inheritance of theme properties, so it's sufficient in
this case to apply element_text() to axis.title and axis.text rather
than to both the x and y versions thereof.)

This would be the 'simple' way to do it. The alternative is to start
playing around in the scales package. A short introduction is given
here: http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf
(see section 7) but some advances have been made since it was written
nearly a year ago. Also see Brian Diggs' posts on defining scales at
the ggplot2 blog:http://blog.ggplot2.org/  The latter of the two posts
is near the top, which contains a link to the first post.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: L-shaped box around plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Johannes,

There is a new theme system that should make this easier. See ?theme
for details, but here is an example:

(p <- ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.border=element_blank(),
        axis.line=element_line()))

my_theme <- theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.border=element_blank(),
        axis.line=element_line())

p + my_theme

messages.subject_clean: Forest plot y-axis in log scale
messages.body_plain:
Thanks a ton Dennis for the solution and also for pointing me to the 'scales' pavkage. That works like a charm.

 -Shubhabrata

On Tuesday, December 18, 2012 11:37:41 PM UTC-8, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> Hi:
>
> This seems to work:
>
> ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, ymin=ylo, ymax=yhi)) +
>     geom_pointrange(size=0.75, shape=18) +
>     geom_hline(yintercept=1, linetype="dashed", lwd=0.7) +
>     scale_y_log10(name="Odds Ratio", limits = c(0.7, 1.8),
>                        breaks=c(0.80, 1.0, 1.20, 1.40, 1.60, 1.80)) +
>     coord_flip() +
> xlab("Study") +
> theme(axis.title = element_text(size=14),
>       axis.text = element_text(face="bold", colour="black"))
>
> If you look carefully, you'll see that the log-transformation is
> applied because the widths between axis ticks on the (log) odds ratio
> scale are not equal. ggplot2 uses the values in the original scale as
> the axis ticks but the scale in which they are rendered is log_10,
> which you can tell by the spacing between the grid lines. See the
> examples at the bottom of
> http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/scale_continuous.html for further
> illustration of this idea.
>
> If you want the plot to be linear in the log10 scale, you could do
> something like this:
>
> ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=log10(y), ymin=log10(ylo), ymax=log10(yhi))) +
>     geom_pointrange(size=0.75, shape=18) +
>     geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed", lwd=0.7) +
>     scale_y_continuous(name="Log Odds Ratio", limits = c(-0.15, 0.25),
>                        breaks= seq(-0.1, 0.2, by = 0.1)) +
>     coord_flip() +
>     xlab("Study") +
>     theme(axis.title = element_text(size=14),
>               axis.text = element_text(face="bold", colour="black"))
>
> (Aside: Notice the abridgement of the theme() call - the new theming
> system applies inheritance of theme properties, so it's sufficient in
> this case to apply element_text() to axis.title and axis.text rather
> than to both the x and y versions thereof.)
>
> This would be the 'simple' way to do it. The alternative is to start
> playing around in the scales package. A short introduction is given
> here: http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf
> (see section 7) but some advances have been made since it was written
> nearly a year ago. Also see Brian Diggs' posts on defining scales at
> the ggplot2 blog:http://blog.ggplot2.org/  The latter of the two posts
> is near the top, which contains a link to the first post.
>
> Dennis
>
> On Tue, Dec 18, 2012 at 5:39 PM, Shubhabrata Mukherjee

messages.subject: GGally::ggpairs questions
messages.body_plain:
I've been playing with 'ggpairs' a bit and have some questions --
perhaps I'm being a bonehead.  If there is a better venue for these
questions (StackOverflow, issues list on github/ggobi/ggally, etc.)
please let me know ...

Here's my basic example:

 library(GGally)
d <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100),]
g1 <- ggpairs(d, columns=5:7, colour="color", shape="cut",
        lower=list(continuous = "smooth"),
        diag=list(continuous="density",discrete="bar"),
        axisLabels="none")

This is mostly OK, but:

0. It took me a while to figure out that non-trivial diagonal subplots
are only produced when axisLabels != "internal" (the default); is this
stated/obviously implied from the documentation, or should I submit an
issue suggesting a doc clarification?

1. I would like to remove the space between the subplots.  My usual
ggplot2 solution to this is:

library(grid)
zmargin <- theme(panel.margin=unit(0,"lines"))
g1 + zmargin

  but this doesn't work in this case (returns NULL).  Suggestions?

2. I would like to set the grouping variable to suppress the
group-by-group display of correlations in the upper panels, densities in
the diagonal panels, and smoothing lines in the lower panels.  I thought
it might be possible to specify the geoms as (e.g.)
geom_smooth(aes(group=1)) , but I get 'Error in subType != "density" :
comparison (2) is possible only for atomic and list types' -- is there
an obvious way to do this?  I also tried this via
params=list(mapping=aes(group=1)) and variations, with no success ..

 OK, I see that I can hack this (following
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/ggplot2/O2o8yaOdLmY ) by
defining a special ggally_function within which I add a geom_smooth()
with an altered grouping:

ggally_spoints <- function(data, mapping, ...){
  p <- ggplot(data = data, mapping = mapping) + geom_point(...) +
     geom_smooth(aes(group=1))
  p$type <- "continuous"
  p$subType <- "points"
  p
}

It should be easy enough to do this with ggally_density as well.  I can
do it with ggally_cor, but I'll have to copy a lot more code ...

  Are there more ggpairs examples somewhere other than

http://sas-and-r.blogspot.ca/2011/12/example-917-much-better-pairs-plots.html
and
example("ggpairs")

  ... ?

  thanks
    Ben Bolker

messages.body_plain:
In an example ( http://rpubs.com/bbolker/3324 ), I wanted to (1)
overlay boxplots and violin plots, (2) use facet_wrap with free scales
to get separate scaling for each variable, (3) lay the figure out
horizontally (i.e. horizontal boxplots and violins).

  I think this is a fairly well known issue, e.g.

https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/95

The last time I encountered this I created a new, horizontal version
of the geom I wanted (I think it was geom_hlinerange), but in this
case I would have to modify both geom_boxplot and geom_violin, and
they're both a bit more complex than linerange (so more chances to
screw up), so I thought I would ask whether a fix was on the horizon
or whether someone else had a workaround that I haven't thought of ...

  thanks
    Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Re: Regression line exceeds confidence band
messages.body_plain:
Because you set the limits with scale_y_continuous, the lowermost
segment of the confidence interval (which would transgress the minimum
y-bound) is getting clipped.  This is standard (if sometimes annoying)
behaviour ... you can either use coord_cartesian() to set the limits, or
library(scales); scale_y_continuous(limits = my_ylim, oob = squish) ...

  Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Re: Regression line exceeds confidence band
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Those were both useful suggestions. The coord_cartesian worked, but it was so precise that it displayed only 1/4 of the extreme point! At first I didn't even realize that the point was there at all. It is almost invisible in the lower left corner. I used a paint package to add an arrow & some text so people would see it.

The squish setting from the scales package did much better, showing the whole point and a bit of axis beyond it. Very nice!  Both plots are attached.

>From help(squish) I never would have guessed it would have this effect. The examples are rather mysterious. Is the oob argument documented anywhere?

Thanks!
Bob
